stories.headline: Elk Fire Grows to Nearly 6,000 Acres, Forces Evacuations Near Lake City
stories.summary:
A lightning-sparked wildfire burning in southwestern Colorado's Hinsdale County expanded dramatically, reaching 5,763 acres — more than 9 square miles — by Friday evening, fire officials said. The Elk Fire is burning approximately one mile northwest of Lake City, a mountain community of about 400 residents in the San Juan Mountains, prompting mandatory evacuations for the San Juan Springs subdivision and placing the entire town under pre-evacuation notice.

Fire officials warned residents at a community meeting Friday night that flying embers could start spot fires in backyards, though the fire would not arrive as a wall of flames. Operations section chief Travis Lipp said crews have plans in place to protect structures, but urged patience, noting the fire will likely burn until snow arrives. Hot, dry and windy conditions Saturday were expected to potentially cause another significant jump in size.

The fire, discovered July 9, stood at 39% containment as of Friday evening. Crews had been pulled away in recent weeks to assist with larger fires in the Pacific Northwest, but Rocky Mountain Complex Incident Management Team 1 ordered a surge in resources, doubling the response team to 104 people and ordering 15 additional engines from across Colorado.

stories.headline: Glenwood Springs Votes 6-1 to Sue Landlord Over ICE Strip-Mall Detention Facility
stories.summary:
The Glenwood Springs City Council voted 6-1 Thursday night to sue the landlord leasing property to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for use as a processing and holding facility. The facility, located between a chiropractor's office and a gym at 100 Midland Ave., has operated for more than 20 years and is used to hold immigrants before transferring them to the state's primary large-scale detention center in Aurora.

The lawsuit centers on zoning violations. Community members, led in part by local attorney Claire Noone, uncovered records indicating immigrants were being held longer than the 12-hour limit established in a decades-old city agreement. The city's planning and zoning commission voted 5-1 in April to revoke the special-use permit enabling ICE to detain people at the address, but enforcement has remained unresolved.

A representative from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security denied that immigrants were held beyond 12 hours at the facility, saying detainees are quickly processed and transferred. The packed council chambers erupted in celebration after the vote, following months of community meetings in which dozens of residents urged the council to take action. Mayor Pro Tem Erin Zalinski acknowledged the delays, saying the council waited until it had a legally defensible course of action.

stories.headline: Kayaker Dies at Eleven Mile Reservoir After Poorly Fitted Life Jacket Covers His Face
stories.summary:
An adult male died Thursday afternoon at Eleven Mile State Park in Park County after strong winds flipped his kayak into the reservoir. Colorado Parks and Wildlife officers responded around 3:30 p.m. and pulled the unconscious man from the water, performing CPR for approximately one hour before he was pronounced dead at the scene shortly after 4:30 p.m.

Officials said the man was wearing a life jacket at the time but it was not properly fitted, and the jacket slid up to cover his face when he entered the water. CPW emphasized that wearing a life jacket is not sufficient — it must be properly buckled or zipped with a snug fit around the abdomen to prevent slippage in the event of an unexpected fall.

The incident also highlighted the danger of sudden, high-wind conditions on Colorado reservoirs, which can overturn watercraft with little warning. The man's identity and official cause of death are to be released by the Park County coroner. CPW used the incident as a reminder to always wear properly fitted personal flotation devices when on or near water.

stories.headline: Gyrocopter Pilot Dies Days After Engine Failure and Crash in Larkspur
stories.summary:
The pilot of a small gyrocopter died after his aircraft's engine failed mid-flight over Larkspur in Douglas County, according to a preliminary report from the National Transportation Safety Board. The pilot had departed Buena Vista on July 13, bound for Peyton, and crashed near the Perry Park Country Club at approximately 8 a.m. after a witness reported hearing the engine struggle and then stop.

The pilot was conscious but unable to speak immediately following the crash and was transported to a hospital, where he died of his injuries five days later. Federal investigators noted the gyrocopter's engine had been operating at an extremely high level prior to the crash. The aircraft was not due for its annual inspection until September, and a friend of the pilot told investigators the gyrocopter had operated smoothly during flights in the days immediately before the fatal trip.

The NTSB continues to investigate the cause of the crash. The preliminary report was published last week, with full findings expected at a later date.

stories.headline: SRM Concrete Buys New Denver Site as Broncos' Burnham Yard Stadium Footprint Clears
stories.summary:
SRM Concrete has purchased $9.45 million in Denver land, a move connected to Denver Broncos owner Greg Penner's efforts to relocate the concrete company whose existing facility sits within the preferred footprint for a proposed Burnham Yard stadium. The land purchase signals progress in clearing the site, which has been a key logistical hurdle in the stadium planning process.

Separately, Denver International Airport is seeking master developers and investment partners to transform approximately 1,500 acres of vacant land adjacent to the airport into mixed-use commercial districts. The airport's development push reflects broader efforts to leverage DIA's land assets for long-term economic growth.

Also in stadium-adjacent news, Denver Summit FC formally submitted its stadium plans to the City and County of Denver for Urban Design review Monday. Updated Urban Design documents list the planned capacity at 12,500 seats, lower than a previously reported figure of 14,500.

stories.headline: Disco Pig Nightclub Closes at Larimer Square, Citing Rising Costs and Declining Foot Traffic
stories.summary:
Disco Pig, a popular nightclub that operated for four years at Larimer Square in downtown Denver, has permanently closed. Operators cited rising operating costs, staffing difficulties and declining foot traffic in the downtown corridor as the primary reasons for the closure.

The closure is the latest in a series of downtown Denver business departures that have underscored ongoing challenges facing the urban core's hospitality and nightlife sectors. Larimer Square, one of Denver's most recognized historic entertainment districts, has seen a number of tenant changes in recent years amid shifting consumer patterns and economic pressures.

No information was immediately available regarding plans for the vacated space. The closure reflects broader trends affecting Denver's nightlife economy, including post-pandemic shifts in how residents engage with downtown entertainment venues.

stories.headline: Denver Metro Home Prices Dip in July, but Luxury Condos Buck the Trend
stories.summary:
The median home price in the 11-county Denver metro area fell 1.54% in July to $605,000, the first across-the-board price decline since early spring, according to the Denver Metro Association of Realtors' monthly Market Trends Report. Detached home prices dropped more than 2% from June to a median of $660,000, while attached homes fell to a median of $380,000, down from $390,000 the previous month.

The exception was the upper end of the condominium market, where sales of attached homes priced above $1 million surged 26% over the month and are up 81% year-over-year. There were 29 such high-end condo sales in July, including a Cherry Creek penthouse at 155 Steele Street that sold for $5.4 million — $150,000 over asking price — in just five days.

Other market indicators also softened, with pending sales falling more than 5%, inventory climbing to nearly 14,000 listings, and the median days on market rising to 21 from 18 in June. Analysts noted that midsummer typically brings slower sales activity as buyers, sellers and agents take vacations.

stories.headline: Denver's City Golf Courses Cut Water Use 20% Amid Drought, Embrace Brown Rough
stories.summary:
All eight of Denver's city-owned golf courses have reduced their water budgets by 20% this summer in response to drought conditions and Denver Water restrictions instituted earlier this year, according to the city's director of agronomy. Staff have prioritized water delivery to tees, fairways and greens, allowing roughs and driving ranges to brown out significantly.

In a normal year, each course requires between 45 million and 65 million gallons of water to maintain green conditions. This year's heat and dryness would have demanded even more water without the cuts, which course managers say they have met through May, June and are on track to meet through July. Mowing schedules have also been reduced, with rough cut once a week instead of twice and shorter grass trimmed twice weekly instead of three times.

City agronomy director Pam Smith, who has managed Denver's golf courses for nearly 20 years, said 2026 may mark a new era of normal for local courses, with golfers in the West needing to adjust expectations around green playing surfaces. Despite the volume reduction, water costs are expected to increase this year because drought-related rate hikes have raised the price of water.

stories.headline: Denver Expands Cooling Center Access Ahead of Weekend Heat Advisory
stories.summary:
The City of Denver widened public access to cooling centers in advance of a forecasted heat advisory, opening some locations Thursday and Friday before the advisory officially went into effect. The move came as the National Weather Service forecast temperatures approaching and potentially exceeding 100 degrees through the weekend.

Denver Gazette weather reporting indicated a high of 97 degrees was expected Friday, just two degrees below the all-time record high for August 7. Wildfire smoke from multiple in-state fires and out-of-state plumes was expected to move in and out throughout the day, with an air quality alert also in effect.

The expanded cooling center access reflects the city's ongoing response to an already historically hot summer. Denver recorded its second-hottest July in city history, and weekend temperatures were forecast to push toward or past the 100-degree threshold again.

stories.headline: Jefferson County Teens Charged After Paddleboarding onto Lake to Flee Burglary Scene
stories.summary:
Two teenage suspects were charged with burglary and criminal trespass after allegedly attempting to escape Jefferson County law enforcement by grabbing paddleboards and heading into the middle of Soda Lakes at Bear Creek Lake Park. The incident began Wednesday when deputies and Lakewood Park Rangers responded to reports of a shirtless male inside the lakeside Soda Lakes Lodge, smashing walls and windows with two-by-fours.

After the two suspects left the building and paddled toward the center of the lake, Lakewood Park Rangers assisted deputies by deploying a patrol boat to make contact with the pair and safely return them to shore. Both were subsequently charged in connection with the burglary and criminal trespass.

All suspects are considered innocent until proven guilty. The Jefferson County Sheriff's Office did not release additional details about the suspects' identities given their status as minors.

stories.headline: Denver Broncos Mascot Miles Inducted into Mascot Hall of Fame
stories.summary:
Miles, the Denver Broncos' official mascot, has been inducted into the Mascot Hall of Fame, recognizing his years of game-day presence and community engagement across Colorado. Miles has been a fixture at Broncos home games and team events, and is frequently involved in charitable outreach throughout the Denver metro area.

The Mascot Hall of Fame recognizes mascots from professional and collegiate sports organizations for their contributions both on the sidelines and in their communities. Miles joins a select group of sports mascots honored for sustained excellence in fan engagement and public service.

The induction adds a distinction to the Broncos organization during an active training camp period, as the team prepares for the upcoming NFL season.

stories.headline: Weekend Events Roundup: Boulder County Fair, Wheat Ridge Carnation Festival, Telluride Jazz and More
stories.summary:
Several notable community events are taking place across the Colorado Front Range and mountains this weekend of August 7-9. The Boulder County Fair continues through Sunday at the Boulder County Fairgrounds in Longmont, featuring carnival rides, a petting zoo, live music and American bull fighters. The Wheat Ridge Carnation Festival at Anderson Park offers a free, family-friendly lineup including a parade, circus, car show, fireworks and carnival rides.

Music fans have multiple options, including the Telluride Jazz Festival at Telluride Town Park, ranked among the world's most scenic music events, and the Beanstalk Music and Mountains Festival in Bond, Colorado, featuring jam-scene acts including Magic Beans and Dogs in a Pile. In Loveland, the 42nd annual Sculpture in the Park runs Friday through Sunday at the Benson Sculpture Garden.

Additional events include the 20th annual Centennial Under the Stars festival Saturday evening at Centennial Center Park, Leadville Boom Days celebrating the town's 1880s mining heritage with burro races and gunslingers, and the Poudre RiverFest in Fort Collins, a free family festival running Saturday from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m.

topStory.headline: Senate Passes Short-Term Funding Bill 90-6 to Avert Government Shutdown Before Midterm Elections
topStory.summary:
The U.S. Senate voted 90-6 in the early hours of Saturday to pass a short-term government funding bill designed to prevent a federal shutdown ahead of the November midterm elections. The legislation, reached through bipartisan negotiation and passed during a late-night session, would extend federal funding at current levels through December 11, providing Congress additional time to negotiate a full-year spending agreement.

The bill includes several provisions added during negotiations, among them a Democratic-backed measure intended to prevent President Donald Trump from withholding federal grants to Democratic-led states for political reasons. The legislation also contains adjustments to protect the SNAP and WIC food assistance programs, along with provisions covering disaster relief and national security funding.

The bill now moves to the House, which must pass it and send it to the president for his signature before September 30 to avert a shutdown beginning October 1. The House had previously passed its own version of a short-term funding measure before the August recess, meaning the two chambers will need to reconcile differences. The Senate adjourned shortly before 5 a.m. ET Saturday and is scheduled to reconvene on September 14.

The wide bipartisan margin in the Senate reflects the political pressure both parties face heading into the November 3 election amid a broad anti-incumbency mood among voters. A government shutdown in the weeks immediately preceding Election Day was seen by members of both parties as a significant political liability, providing strong incentive to reach agreement quickly.
